sources.title: South Sudan: South Sudan Rejects Claims of Foreigners' Expulsion Order
sources.excerpt: [Capital FM] Nairobi -- South Sudan has moved to dispel reports that foreigners have been given seven days to leave the country, with Juba County Caretaker Commissioner Kalisto Lado Faustino Nyigilo saying the government remains open to legally resident foreigners but wants them to stay out of small-scale retail…
sources.text: South Sudan: South Sudan Rejects Claims of Foreigners' Expulsion Order. Nairobi — South Sudan has moved to dispel reports that foreigners have been given seven days to leave the country, with Juba County Caretaker Commissioner Kalisto Lado Faustino Nyigilo saying the government remains open to legally resident foreigners but wants them to stay out of small-scale retail businesses. Lado made the clarification on Tuesday following reports circulating on social media claiming that he had ordered foreign nationals to leave South Sudan. He said the reports were false and that he did not have the authority to expel foreigners from the country. "The Commissioner has never said that, and it's even not the mandate of the Commissioner to actually evacuate people or to send people out of South Sudan," Lado said. He said South Sudan welcomes foreigners who enter the country legally for business, residence, humanitarian work and other legitimate activities. "Our policy is welcoming. We are welcoming everybody from any country who want to come to be with us in South Sudan," he said. However, Lado maintained his position that foreign nationals should avoid small-scale retail trade in Juba, including boda boda operations and the sale of everyday food items. He said foreigners should instead invest in wholesale businesses, companies, factories and other ventures capable of creating jobs for South Sudanese. Lado said his earlier remarks were aimed at protecting economic opportunities for local youth and women rather than discriminating against foreigners. He questioned the growing involvement of foreign nationals in boda boda operations, asking what opportunities would remain for South Sudanese youth if foreigners dominated the sector. He similarly raised concern over foreign women engaging in small-scale food vending, including selling chapati, potatoes, onions and tomatoes. Lado rejected claims that his position amounted to a ban on foreign investment or hostility towards foreigners. "There is nothing about sending of foreigners out of South Sudan. There is nothing about prohibiting foreigners from business. There is nothing about hating foreigners," he said. He instead urged foreign investors to bring substantial capital into the country and establish industries and companies that could employ South Sudanese. Lado also addressed the ongoing removal of roadside businesses and structures in Juba, saying the county was not conducting indiscriminate demolitions. He said the exercise was intended to clear roads, remove garbage and relocate businesses operating on road reserves to designated areas. To complete the process, please follow the instructions in the email we just sent you. There was a problem processing your submission. Please try again later. "We are not demolishing structures. We are organising the road, taking garbage out of the road and sending those who are putting their booths on the road to be in the rightful places," he said. Lado urged foreigners living in Juba to remain calm, saying those who obey South Sudanese laws had nothing to fear. "Our foreigners who are here, be peaceful. No fear, no worry, unless if you commit any crime," he said. sources.title: South Sudan’s aid crisis deepens as food stocks run low
sources.excerpt: More than one million people could lose life-saving aid by October as funding shrinks and arrivals from Sudan continue.
sources.text: South Sudan’s aid crisis deepens as food stocks run low. More than one million vulnerable people could lose access to life-saving food and nutrition assistance by October unless additional resources are secured, according to the World Food Programme (WFP). In Malakal, one of the agency’s key logistics hubs in the Upper Nile state, food stocks have fallen from 10,000 metric tonnes at this time last year to less than 300 tonnes now. The drop comes as humanitarian agencies face shrinking resources while needs continue to rise, WFP says. WFP assistant executive director Matthew Hollingworth visited Renk and Malakal in Upper Nile and Pigi county in Jonglei state this month, where he witnessed firsthand the pressures facing communities already struggling with conflict, displacement, hunger and climate shocks. Hollingworth told Al Jazeera that the war in Sudan had driven up prices and put additional pressure on a country already stretched by the influx of refugees. “The war in Sudan has been catastrophic for the north of this country. Prices have gone so much higher due to the complexity of importing goods from Sudan,” he said. “Moreover, the influx of refugees [comes] to a country that is really stretched when it comes to helping them.” In Renk, Hollingworth saw the effects of drought alongside areas still affected by flooding. “It all comes at the time when the international community has a lot less to give, and we don’t have the same resources we used to have,” he told Al Jazeera. “On the other side, the government of South Sudan has to consider the issue of illegal checkpoints that prevent us from being able to get everywhere. We need to reach vulnerable people across the country.” Peter Maker, a displaced person in Pigi, said insecurity and the arrival of people displaced from other areas had made it difficult to farm or find work. “We face major challenges due to national insecurity and an influx of people from other areas. Our main issues are insecurity and lack of access to farmland,” he told Al Jazeera. “Although I am able-bodied and qualified to work, insecurity prevents me from travelling for opportunities or farming safely outside, leaving us heavily reliant on the UN and aid.” Maker said longer-term solutions were needed and warned that further cuts or blockages to assistance would be devastating. He attributed much of the local suffering to political leadership and divisions between communities, while saying people currently survive by sharing resources, relying on God and receiving occasional aid. Renk, in Upper Nile state near the border with Sudan, has become a major entry point for people fleeing the war that erupted there in April 2023. More than 1.4 million refugees and returnees have crossed into South Sudan since the war erupted in Sudan in 2023, according to the World Food Programme. Many arrive after journeys marked by checkpoints, extortion and violence, with little idea of what comes next. Zainab Musa, a mother of six staying at a transit centre in Renk, recently crossed from Sudan. She said conditions were difficult and there was little food. “The humanitarian situation is hard and there is nothing to eat, just hunger,” she told Al Jazeera. “I thought of moving from the border at Jodha to the transit centre to look for help.” Musa said she planned to travel to her grandfather in Bunj, in Maban county, in Upper Nile. The transit centres in Renk were not designed for the scale of arrivals they are now receiving. Families wait for onward transport to Malakal or other parts of South Sudan, while some remain for months. The WFP has been forced to reduce rations and cut support as funding has dried up. In August, the WFP and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) warned that more than 650,000 refugees and asylum seekers were at risk of losing food assistance. They said food and nutrition assistance for the most vulnerable 240,000 refugees was expected to run out in September without additional funding. Nura Mohammed Ahmed, a Sudanese refugee, said hunger and a lack of adequate nutrition were already taking a heavy toll at the transit centre. Malakal has hosted families displaced by conflict and disaster for years. The former Protection of Civilians site, redesignated as an internally displaced people’s settlement earlier this year, hosts nearly 40,000 displaced people across more than 6,000 households. Many have been displaced for years. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that water, sanitation and hygiene services in Bentiu and Malakal are at risk because of funding shortfalls. Without drainage pumping and dyke maintenance, Malakal also faces a heightened risk of flooding during the rainy season. Najah al-Tayieb al-Fadhul, a Sudanese refugee and mother of four, arrived at a transit centre in December 2023 after her husband was killed. “My husband was killed by the Sudan armed forces in front of me, and I could not stay with my kids there because the situation was traumatising,” she told Al Jazeera. “I entered South Sudan, and I have tried my best to hustle and earn some small job with the humanitarian organisations based in Renk.” Al-Fadhul said hunger, sickness and malnutrition were part of daily life. “There are massive cases of hunger, sickness and malnutrition among the children,” she said. “Even my child has a heart disease, and I cannot afford to treat him.” She said she sometimes earned about $2.50 a day from work in the market, but struggled to find stable employment despite having a college degree. “The humanitarian situation is worsening despite securing a job with one of the organisations,” she said. “WFP only helped us here with the small ration for the children in particular. Elders and most individuals lack energy to work due to hunger.” The WFP says it faces an immediate $86m funding gap and a $416m shortfall over the next six months, threatening its ability to assist refugees, displaced people and vulnerable host communities. sources.title: Christian Workers Abducted in South Sudan Are Released
sources.excerpt: Six Christian workers in South Sudan were released after five days of captivity marked by beatings and harsh conditions.
sources.text: Christian Workers Abducted in South Sudan Are Released. Six Christian workers abducted in South Sudan on Sept. 26 were released on Thursday (Oct. 1), sources said. The Young Life South Sudan workers were traveling from Kajo Keji to Maridi, a town in Western Equatoria state, on Juba-Yambio Road when unidentified gunmen ambushed their vehicle, the ministry’s country director, Pastor David Nyoma John, told Morning Star News. “On Sept. 26, at about 9:45 p.m., our young life leaders from Maridi were ambushed along the Juba-Yambio Road while returning from theological education in Kajo Keji,” Pastor John said. “They were taken by unknown armed group and held for about five days in the far bush under harsh conditions.” The abducted workers reported that they were beaten, forced to carry heavy loads for long distances and were not given adequate food and water. They were made to sleep in the open without shelter or bedding. The assailants confiscated their personal belongings, including mobile phones, Bibles and theological training certificates, Pastor John said, adding that the workers were traumatized and required psychosocial and medical care. The workers, all native South Sudanese, were identified as Thomas Oliver, Japheth Elisama, John Simon, Justin Wilson, James Banyi, and Ezibon Yoanna. It was not immediately clear why they were released, but it appeared they were abducted as a form of punishment for their ministry. Order Abby Trivett’s New Book, “The Power of Suddenly” on Amazon.com! Catholic Bishop of Tombura-Yambio Diocese Eduardo Hiinoro Kussala condemned the kidnapping and other attacks on civilians and called the armed groups to stop targeting civilians. “Those people whom you are ambushing are your brothers are your citizens,” he told a Juba radio station, Eye Radio. “They are your brothers and sisters.” South Sudan’s population is 63.7 percent Christian, 26.9 percent adherents of ethnic religion and 8.8 percent Muslim, according to the Joshua Project. The world’s youngest country after gaining independence from Sudan in July 2011, South Sudan saw civil war erupt in 2013. Fighting continues despite a 2018 peace agreement, according to the United Nations , and renewed violence, political tensions, corruption and impunity leave many people at risk. Christians have been targeted in the country. On Feb. 25, the body of a church pastor near Juba was found after he had been abducted on Feb. 19. The body of Pastor Lino Pasquale of Hai Baraka Pentecostal Church was found after he was abducted while fishing at a river in Gondokoro, 10 kilometers (six miles) from Juba. He was “targeted and killed by unknown gunmen,” according to leaders of the Sudan Pentecostal Church (SPC). The killing was not an isolated incident. On Jan. 14, the Rev. Christopher Maring, a senior leader within the Africa Inland Church (AIC), was assassinated, according to AIC Deputy Presiding Bishop Martin Mogga. Pastor Maring was shot and killed at approximately 7:30 p.m. at his home in the Gudele suburb by unidentified gunmen, they said. Church leaders in the region are increasingly calling for better protection and investigations into targeted killings, as the motives behind the attacks remain officially “unidentified” by local authorities. sources.title: South Africa: President Ramaphosa meets President Salva Kiir of South Sudan
sources.excerpt: President Cyril Ramaphosa has this afternoon met with His Excellency Salva Kiir Mayardit, President of the Republic of South Sudan, in Pretoria, South Africa. President Salva Kiir Mayardit is in South ...
sources.text: South Africa: President Ramaphosa meets President Salva Kiir of South Sudan. President Cyril Ramaphosa has this afternoon met with His Excellency Salva Kiir Mayardit, President of the Republic of South Sudan, in Pretoria, South Africa. President Salva Kiir Mayardit is in South Africa on a working visit. During their discussions, President Ramaphosa emphasised the importance of full adherence to the Revitalised Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in the Republic of South Sudan (R ARCSS), as a means to advance the peace process and consolidate progress towards lasting peace and stability in South Sudan. President Ramaphosa underscored the need for an inclusive electoral process predicated on mutual trust and cooperation among South Sudanese stakeholders to address outstanding challenges and create an enabling environment for the effective implementation of the peace agreement, especially towards the lead up the December elections. The meeting reaffirmed the significance of sustained regional engagement and collaboration in support of peace, stability and political progress in South Sudan, including electoral capacity support from the C5 countries. sources.title: Bianchi Gold Deal Signals Broadening Investor Base in South Sudan’s Oil Sector Ahead of South Sudan Oil & Power (SSOP) 2026
sources.excerpt: A strategic investment memorandum signed between South Sudan’s Ministry of Petroleum and UAE-based Bianchi Gold Trading Investment Company is highlighting the country’s efforts to attract new ...
sources.text: Bianchi Gold Deal Signals Broadening Investor Base in South Sudan’s Oil Sector Ahead of South Sudan Oil & Power (SSOP) 2026. A strategic investment memorandum signed between South Sudan’s Ministry of Petroleum and UAE-based Bianchi Gold Trading Investment Company is highlighting the country’s efforts to attract new international partners as it seeks to expand investment across its oil and gas sector ahead of South Sudan Oil&Power (SSOP) 2026. Signed in Juba on July 8, the MoU establishes cooperation between the Ministry and Bianchi Gold across petroleum exploration and development, oil and gas infrastructure, refining, storage and distribution, feasibility studies and capacity building. The partnership is intended to mobilize financial and technical resources to support the development and modernization of South Sudan’s petroleum industry. The agreement comes as South Sudan seeks to expand investment beyond its existing producing assets and attract partners capable of bringing capital, technology and expertise to new developments. The country currently has 14 open concession blocks spanning the A, B, C, D and E areas, building on the five blocks offered in South Sudan’s first-ever oil licensing round in 2021. The opportunity extends beyond exploration and production. Cooperation covering refining, storage and distribution could support the development of domestic and midstream infrastructure, while technical studies and capacity building could help strengthen local capabilities and service provision across the sector. South Sudan’s resource base provides a substantial platform for this investment drive. SSOP 2026 highlights 3.5 billion barrels of proven oil reserves, with nearly 90% described as untapped, and the government targeting production of 230,000 barrels per day in the short term and 450,000 barrels per day over the longer term. Against this backdrop, the Bianchi partnership offers a timely example of the type of international investment and technical collaboration South Sudan is seeking to attract. The country’s seventh South Sudan Oil&Power (SSOP) conference, taking place in Juba on November 24–25, will bring together government, investors, financiers, project developers and technology providers to advance partnerships across upstream oil and gas, refining, midstream infrastructure and power. For South Sudan, the focus now is on converting its resource base into production, infrastructure and wider economic value. As SSOP 2026 approaches, partnerships such as the Bianchi MoU underscore the country’s drive to attract the capital, technology and expertise needed to advance that next phase of development. sources.title: Canada helping to fund South Sudan vote despite growing repression
sources.excerpt: The much-delayed election would be the first since South Sudan achieved independence in 2011. Canada has spent more than $1.1-billion in foreign aid supporting the country since then, but its ...
sources.text: Canada helping to fund South Sudan vote despite growing repression. The much-delayed election would be the first since South Sudan achieved independence in 2011. Canada has spent more than $1.1-billion in foreign aid supporting the country since then, but its government has continued to jail opponents and entrench power in the hands of President Salva Kiir and his family. “Many of the safeguards and conditions for peaceful and credible polls are still missing,” United Nations human-rights commissioner Barney Afako warned after a visit to the country last month. “Political and civic space has narrowed.” If the election goes ahead without the conditions needed for free participation, it could “fuel renewed conflict and increase the risk of atrocity crimes,” the commission said in a report. Global Affairs Canada says it is contributing about $1.3-million to a UN-managed fund to support electoral preparedness in South Sudan, including voter education and community peacebuilding. But the department says it is deeply concerned about the election, including unresolved security problems, delays in the country’s peace agreement and restrictions on civic and political space – “all of which could affect the credibility of the electoral process,” Global Affairs spokesperson Renelle Arsenault told The Globe and Mail. South Sudan was strongly supported by Western governments when it separated from Sudan, becoming the world’s newest country. But war erupted in 2013, killing hundreds of thousands of people, and clashes have continued in recent years despite a 2018 peace agreement. Elections in the impoverished country have been repeatedly postponed, allowing Mr. Kiir to remain in power. Much of the violent conflict is between factions aligned with Mr. Kiir and those backing his rival, Riek Machar, who has been vice-president for most of the past 15 years. Last year, Mr. Machar was arrested, suspended from his post and charged with treason. He remains on trial today. The government is pushing ahead with the election despite the absence of a national census or a permanent constitution, both of which were listed as electoral requirements in the 2018 peace deal. There is also no voter registry, which casts further doubt on the election. “Any endorsement by international partners for holding elections under current political conditions would be counterproductive,” said a report last month by Guyo Chepe Turi and Said Abdullahi, two researchers at the Africa-based Institute for Security Studies. “It would signal acquiescence in dismantling the 2018 deal, risking a reversal of hard-won progress.” Any future Canadian support for the election will depend on the status of the peace agreement, the political and security situation, the inclusiveness and credibility of the electoral process and whether the conditions are in place to ensure that the vote contributes to peace and stability, Ms. Arsenault said. Canada is not the only country to voice its concern. The head of the European Union delegation to South Sudan, Pelle Enarsson, said the EU has not yet allocated any funds to support the vote because the government has not disclosed a clear budget or plan. Funding would depend on whether the electoral process is inclusive and credible, he told journalists recently. Last month, Mr. Kiir dismantled the unity government – a power-sharing arrangement from the peace agreement − and appointed a new government filled with his loyalists. He has promoted his son, Major-General Atem Salva Kiir, to command the elite Presidential Guard, known as the Tiger Division, and has named other family members to senior posts in the Defence Department and the National Election Commission. These moves have triggered alarm that his aim is to “consolidate power with the goal of managing a dynastic succession,” International Crisis Group analyst Daniel Akech said in a report this week. Since its independence, South Sudan has received more than US$23-billion in oil revenue and US$27-billion in foreign aid from donors, but it remains one of the world’s poorest countries, largely because predatory officials have looted billions of dollars, a UN commission reported last year. Violent conflict, meanwhile, has pushed millions of people from their homes. A senior official of the World Food Programme, Matthew Hollingworth, said last month that the situation is “catastrophic,” with 7.8 million South Sudanese – almost two-thirds of the population – struggling daily to find enough food to survive. Because of widespread cuts in donor assistance over the past year, the budgets of relief agencies are rapidly declining and “about to drop off the financial cliff,” Mr. Hollingworth said. “The government of South Sudan has to start mobilizing their own funds to support their own people.”

sources.title: South Sudan steps up Ebola alert after Kenya case
sources.excerpt: South Sudan has stepped up nationwide preparedness and surveillance against Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus after neighboring Kenya confirmed an imported case, the Ministry of Health said ...
sources.text: South Sudan steps up Ebola alert after Kenya case. JUBA, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- South Sudan has stepped up nationwide preparedness and surveillance against Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus after neighboring Kenya confirmed an imported case, the Ministry of Health said on Wednesday. No cases have been detected in the country and the health system has been placed on high alert, according to the ministry. The ministry said this heightened posture is a proactive response to increased regional mobility and vital trade corridors linking South Sudan with affected areas in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as well as key transit routes through Kenya and Uganda. "The geographical expansion of the outbreak to Kenya further increases the risk of cross-border spread and underscores the urgent need for heightened vigilance at points of entry," Caretaker Minister for Health Dak Duop Bichiok told a press conference in Juba, the capital. The ministry said South Sudan has reactivated its Ebola preparedness and response system, with screening being conducted at points of entry, along the border in 15 high-risk counties and at Juba International Airport. Ader Machar Aciek, acting executive director of the National Public Health Institute, announced that a dedicated national task force has been established and is convening regular sessions to coordinate ongoing preparedness operations. Aciek noted that South Sudan has established eight specialized infectious disease units dedicated to isolation and clinical case management should any cases be confirmed. Moses Ongom, World Health Organization (WHO) Officer in Charge in South Sudan, said that national response preparedness has climbed significantly, rising from 29 percent in May and 45 percent in June to 65 percent currently. Ongom emphasized that infectious disease control units and response capabilities have been reinforced in priority zones, while urging local communities to remain vigilant and immediately report suspected cases. Tolbert Geewleh Nyenswah, country director for the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) in South Sudan, said the country has active systems for surveillance, detection, rapid response and laboratory testing. Nyenswah added that the Africa CDC and the WHO are actively coordinating a regional incident management support mechanism based in Kampala. Nyenswah said the mechanism is designed to strengthen cross-border cooperation among countries affected by or bordering the DRC. The Ministry of Health has urged the public to remain calm yet vigilant, practice regular hand hygiene, and avoid direct contact with individuals exhibiting symptoms associated with Ebola. It said anyone with suspected symptoms, including fever, vomiting, diarrhea or unexplained bleeding, should report to the nearest health facility or call the toll-free emergency hotline 6666. ■

sources.title: South Sudan Explained 2026, the World’s Youngest Country
sources.excerpt: South Sudan explained: an oil-producing, landlocked state of over 10 million people faces a 22 December 2026 election under a caretaker government.
sources.text: South Sudan Explained 2026, the World’s Youngest Country. South Sudan explained: it is the world’s youngest country, an oil-producing and landlocked state whose political transition remains unfinished. President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government and appointed a caretaker administration on September 22, 2026; elections are scheduled for December 22, 2026. South Sudan sits in East-Central Africa, bordered by Sudan, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Central African Republic. This guide explains its geography, people, political system, economy, daily life and what to watch in 2026. South Sudan is a presidential republic that has never fully consolidated its constitutional order. It became independent from Sudan on July 9, 2011, after a referendum in which southern voters overwhelmingly supported separation. The official language is English, and the capital is Juba, on the White Nile in Central Equatoria. The country is landlocked. It borders Sudan to the north, Ethiopia to the east, Kenya and Uganda to the southeast, the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the southwest, and the Central African Republic to the west. Its territory is dominated by broad savannahs, wetlands and seasonal floodplains. The most distinctive physical feature is the Sudd, one of the world’s largest tropical wetlands. The White Nile and its tributaries shape transport, agriculture, livestock movements and settlement patterns. Seasonal flooding can isolate communities for months, while roads become difficult or impossible to use during the rainy season. South Sudan is divided into 10 states and several administrative areas, including Abyei, Greater Pibor and Ruweng. However, the national government dissolved the state governments and legislative assemblies in September 2026 as part of the caretaker arrangement. Juba remains the political and commercial centre, while other important towns include Wau, Malakal, Bor, Yambio, Aweil and Rumbek. South Sudan’s independence in 2011 followed decades of conflict between Sudan’s central government and southern armed movements. The 2018 peace agreement, formally implemented in February 2020, created the Revitalized Transitional Government of National Unity. That arrangement brought President Salva Kiir Mayardit’s Sudan People’s Liberation Movement together with opposition groups led by Riek Machar and other parties. Under the transitional arrangement, executive power was concentrated in the presidency and a group of vice presidents representing the major peace-agreement parties. Before the September 2026 dissolution, the vice-presidential offices listed by the Ministry of Justice were held by Riek Machar Teny Dhurgon as First Vice President, James Wani Igga, Taban Deng Gai, Rebecca Nyandeng De Mabior and Hussein Abdelbagi Akol as vice presidents. That arrangement changed materially in September 2026. President Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government, the national legislature, the state governments and the state assemblies. He also relieved the first vice president and the other vice presidents of their positions. The decree established a caretaker administration, with government ministries and institutions instructed to continue operating under interim arrangements until elected institutions take office. South Sudan has a highly diverse population, with many ethnic groups and languages. The largest communities commonly identified in political and demographic discussions include the Dinka, Nuer, Shilluk, Bari, Azande, Anyuak, Murle, Kakwa, Luo and Jie, among others. Ethnicity, locality, cattle ownership, political allegiance and access to land all influence social and political life. Ethnic identity is not simply cultural. During periods of conflict, political competition has often been organised through ethnic and regional networks. Christianity and traditional African religions are widespread, while Islam is especially present in northern and border communities. Religious affiliation varies significantly by region and community. English is the official working language of government and formal education. Arabic, particularly Juba Arabic, is widely used in daily commerce and inter-community communication. Numerous local languages remain central to family, community and cultural life. The population is young, rural and highly mobile. Many people have been displaced internally or have crossed into neighbouring countries as refugees. The World Bank projected that more than 10 million people, about two-thirds of the population, would require humanitarian assistance during 2026. This figure describes a country where formal institutions and modern services exist but are unevenly distributed and often depend on private providers, humanitarian agencies or international organisations. South Sudan’s political framework remains transitional rather than fully consolidated. As of October 3, 2026, President Salva Kiir Mayardit remains in office, while a caretaker administration oversees the country ahead of elections scheduled for December 22, 2026. The September 2026 legal changes allowed President Kiir to remain in office during the election period and removed the vice-presidential arrangement created by the 2018 peace agreement. The caretaker government is not the same as the pre-September transitional cabinet. The September order named caretaker officials for the main portfolios, including Africano Mande Gedima (Presidential Affairs), Martin Elia Lomuro (Cabinet Affairs), Cecilia Adut Manyok (Foreign Affairs), Ayor Akuoch Anok (Defence), Rizik Zachariah Hassan (Interior), Wek Mamer Kuol (Justice), Obote Mamur Mete (National Security), Athian Diing Athian (Finance), Awow Daniel Chuang (Petroleum), Labanya Margret (Trade) and Ateny Wek Ateny (Information and ICT). These appointments should be treated as current caretaker offices, not as evidence that the country has returned to a normal post-election constitutional system. sources.text: South Sudan oil is being used as a political weapon, expert says. South Sudan’s oil has become a strategic tool in the war in neighbouring Sudan, with competing sides using access to the country’s crude as leverage, according to Professor Taj Elkhazin, a Sudan and South Sudan researcher. Elkhazin, an associate professor at the Norman Paterson School of International Affairs at Carleton University in Ottawa, said the country’s dependence on Sudan’s oil infrastructure had left Juba vulnerable to pressure from both the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). He told Radio Tamazuj on Thursday that South Sudan’s oil is increasingly being used for political and military purposes rather than to meet the needs of its population. “The issue of oil is a classical case of mismanagement and a classical case of corruption,” he said. His comments come as South Sudan prepares for planned elections in December, while fighting in Sudan continues to affect border areas and the pipeline infrastructure through which South Sudan exports most of its crude. Elkhazin said that South Sudan oil transported through Sudan is currently generating revenue for both the army-aligned government in Khartoum and the RSF despite the two sides being at war. He said information from people he described as insiders indicated that about $4 from each barrel of crude oil goes to RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti, while about $6 goes to the Sudanese army. The RSF seized Heglig on 8 December 2025, prompting South Sudan to deploy troops to secure the strategic oil field. Heglig, in Sudan’s South Kordofan state near the South Sudan border, is a key oil-processing site for South Sudanese crude. Elkhazin also alleged that the South Sudanese government had recently requested $20 million from Hemedti and that the money was delivered in cash by plane. In return, he said, the RSF received two shipments of South Sudanese crude, each involving about 600,000 barrels. Radio Tamazuj could not independently verify the alleged payment or the shipments. South Sudan’s crude is exported through infrastructure in Sudan to the Red Sea. The Bashair oil terminals, located south of Port Sudan, are key parts of Sudan’s oil-export infrastructure. Elkhazin said the oil arrangement creates a dangerous dependency because Sudan could disrupt South Sudan’s exports by restricting access to the pipeline and export terminals. Elkhazin, who is also a water management expert, revisited a 2022 dispute over Egyptian equipment brought into South Sudan for work on the Bahr al-Ghazal Basin. He said he had been personally invited by President Salva Kiir Mayardit to advise the South Sudanese government on water management and that a team of South Sudanese and international experts spent five days examining the issue. According to Elkhazin, the team produced a report dated 27 July 2022 that was subsequently presented to the Council of Ministers. He said the equipment brought from Egypt was intended for dredging rather than simply clearing vegetation from waterways. “Dredging” involves deepening or altering the riverbed to increase the capacity and flow of water, while routine clearing involves removing vegetation from the surface, he said. Elkhazin said that members of the Misseriya community in Sudan intercepted the Egyptian equipment convoy and were paid $50,000 to allow it to proceed. He said the equipment eventually reached the Bahr al-Ghazal Basin, where dredging took place before being returned to Egypt. He also claimed that vegetation removed during the operation contributed to flooding around the old bridge at Kosti in Sudan. Elkhazin said the report produced by his team remains largely unused. Elkhazin also alleged that about 450 RSF personnel are stationed near Juba. He said the declared purpose of the deployment was to assist with stabilization and preparations for South Sudan’s elections. But he questioned why foreign armed personnel would be needed for such duties while South Sudan has its own security forces. He argued that the presence of the RSF was instead intended to help protect the government of President Kiir. “The declared mission was to help with some stabilisation and help with the upcoming elections,” he said. “However, you do not bring forces from outside to your country while you have an army to do that.” Elkhazin further alleged that supplies are moving from or through Juba towards RSF-held areas in Sudan. He said he had seen a United Nations report which, in his interpretation, traced the movement of oil and other supplies through South Sudan towards areas controlled by the RSF. He warned that the fighting in Sudan could increasingly spill across the border and complicate South Sudan’s security and economic interests. Turning to South Sudan’s planned elections, Elkhazin questioned whether a credible vote could be held without a national census. “No census has been done in South Sudan for years now,” he said, arguing that uncertainty over the size and location of the population could create opportunities for manipulation. He also criticised the political and security environment ahead of the elections, pointing to the detention and trial of opposition leader Riek Machar and recent political appointments and dismissals. The country’s transitional government was dissolved by President Kiir on 22 September, although the president said the administration would continue in a caretaker capacity until elected leaders take office. Elkhazin argued that the broader political environment is not conducive to what he described as fair and credible elections. He accused the government of using political appointments and dismissals to divert public attention from deeper governance problems. “The whole scenario now has become what we call a political stunt,” he said. Elkhazin also warned that the conflict in Sudan is likely to continue unless the two main warring sides—the Sudanese Armed Forces and the RSF—are brought into a comprehensive political settlement. sources.text: South Sudan. South Sudan, officially the Republic of South Sudan, is a landlocked country in East Africa. It is bordered by Sudan to the north, Ethiopia to the east, Kenya to the southeast, Uganda to the south, the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the southwest, and the Central African Republic to the west. South Sudan's diverse landscape includes vast plains and plateaus, dry and tropical savannahs, inland floodplains, and forested mountains. The Nile River system is the defining physical feature of the country, running south to north across its center, which is dominated by a large swamp known as the Sudd. South Sudan has an estimated population of just over 12.7 million in 2024. Juba is the capital and largest city.
